summary.text: The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality is an upper bound on the absolute value of the inner product of two vectors, set by the product of the vectors' norms.
The two sides are equal if and only if the two vectors are linearly dependent.
It is considered one of the most important and widely used inequalities in mathematics, with uses from graph theory to the spectral theorem.

facts.label: Integral version
facts.value: Published by Bunyakovsky in 1859 and Schwarz in 1888

facts.label: Equality case
facts.value: Both sides match only for linearly dependent vectors

facts.label: Graph theory use
facts.value: Proves Mantel's theorem on triangle-free graphs

facts.label: Angle idea
facts.value: Lets angles between vectors work in any real inner-product space

items.prompt: Two arrows drawn on a flat sheet of paper point in exactly opposite directions. How do the two sides of the inequality compare for this pair?

options.label: The left side is strictly smaller
The two sides are equal
The left side is strictly larger
The sides cannot be compared for opposite arrows

items.explain: In the plane, equality holds when the vectors point in the same or opposite directions, or when one of them is the zero vector.

items.prompt: For a particular pair of vectors, the product of their lengths turns out to be strictly bigger than the absolute value of their inner product. What follows?

options.label: The vectors must both be the zero vector
The inequality has failed for this pair
The vectors must have equal lengths
The vectors are not linearly dependent

items.explain: The two sides are equal if and only if the vectors are linearly dependent, so a strict gap means they are not.

items.prompt: A student has the inequality for lists of numbers and wants it for areas under curves. Why can the same idea cover both?

options.label: Areas under curves are always just lists of numbers
Integrals are a type of vector, so the inequality was never needed
Inner products of vectors can describe sums, series and integrals
The sum version has to be applied twice for any integral

items.explain: Inner products can describe finite sums, infinite series and integrals, and the inequality holds for these inner products.

items.prompt: In the study of graphs with no triangles, what role does this inequality play?

options.label: It colours the points so no triangle appears
It counts every triangle exactly
It shows every large graph must contain a triangle
It is used to prove a cap on how many edges such a graph can have

items.explain: It is used to prove Mantel's theorem, which bounds the number of edges in a triangle-free graph.

items.prompt: You find a proof of this inequality written only for the real numbers. What should you keep in mind when using it?

options.label: It automatically covers every inner product space
It might not be valid when the field is the complex numbers
It is wrong, because proofs must work over complex numbers
It only needs checking when one vector is zero

items.explain: Some proofs are only valid when the field is the real numbers and not the complex numbers, a common source of confusion.

paragraphs.heading: A ceiling on inner products
paragraphs.text: The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, also called the Cauchy–Bunyakovsky–Schwarz inequality, puts an upper limit on the inner product of two vectors. It says the absolute value of that inner product can be no bigger than the product of the two vectors' norms. It is counted among the most important and most widely used inequalities in mathematics. Since inner products can stand for finite sums, infinite series or integrals, the one statement covers all three.

paragraphs.heading: Who found it
paragraphs.text: Augustin-Louis Cauchy published the version for sums in 1821. The matching inequality for integrals was published by Viktor Bunyakovsky in 1859 and by Hermann Schwarz in 1888. Schwarz also gave the modern proof of that integral version.

paragraphs.heading: Picture it in the plane
paragraphs.text: In the flat plane ℝ², the inner product is the ordinary dot product. There the inequality says (‖𝐮‖‖𝐯‖cos θ)² can be at most ‖𝐮‖²‖𝐯‖², with θ standing for the angle that separates the two vectors. This may be the easiest form to grasp: the square of a cosine is never more than 1, and it reaches 1 when the vectors point the same way or opposite ways.

paragraphs.heading: When the two sides match
paragraphs.text: In coordinates, with 𝐮 = (u₁, u₂) and 𝐯 = (v₁, v₂), the inequality reads (u₁v₁ + u₂v₂)² ≤ (u₁² + u₂²)(v₁² + v₂²). The two sides are equal only if the vectors line up in the same or opposite directions, or one of them is the zero vector. In general, the two sides match exactly when the vectors are linearly dependent.

paragraphs.heading: Angles in any space
paragraphs.text: One payoff is a meaning for the angle between two vectors in any real inner-product space. You define cos θ_𝐮𝐯 = (⟨𝐮, 𝐯⟩)/‖𝐮‖‖𝐯‖, and Cauchy–Schwarz shows the right-hand side always lies between −1 and 1, so the definition makes sense. That supports the view that real Hilbert spaces are simply generalizations of Euclidean space.

paragraphs.heading: Where it gets used
paragraphs.text: The inequality has many uses. It proves that the inner product is a continuous function, and it can prove the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators in finite dimensions. In probability, defining the inner product of two random variables as the expectation of their product turns it into |E (XY)| ² ≤ E (X²)E (Y²). In graph theory it proves Mantel's theorem: a graph on n vertices with no triangles has at most ⌊1/4n²⌋ edges.
